items.a: Usually at the start, but not automatically forever. As of 26 September 2026, WooCommerce's core plugin costs $0, with no plan tiers and no cut of sales, while Shopify's cheapest plan, Basic, costs $39 a month. WooCommerce still needs hosting, though, and a budget host such as Pressable starts around $25 a month, which is below Shopify's Basic price. The gap tends to hold as a team grows too, mainly because Shopify charges more once a store needs extra staff logins, while WooCommerce's WordPress user accounts stay free at any size. WooCommerce's price advantage narrows once a store adds paid extensions: common ones such as WooCommerce Subscriptions or Bookings cost $279 and $249 a year, on top of hosting, and two or three of those can close most of the gap to Shopify's Grow or Advanced plans.

items.q: Can I switch from Shopify to WooCommerce, or the other way, later?
items.a: Yes, but expect to rebuild the storefront, not just move a file. Both platforms let you export your product catalog to a CSV file, so your product data usually survives a move. What does not move is the storefront and checkout code: a Shopify store only runs on Shopify's own servers, and a WooCommerce store is built as WordPress code and templates, so switching between them means recreating the theme, checkout flow and any custom logic on the new platform. WooCommerce does have one advantage after you are on it: because it is your own WordPress site, you can change hosts whenever you want without touching the storefront at all, which a Shopify store cannot do. Budget real time for a full switch in either direction, not a quick import.

items.q: Do I need to know how to code to run a WooCommerce store?
items.a: Not to launch a standard one. A managed host that installs WordPress and WooCommerce together, such as WordPress.com's Commerce plan, lets you pick a theme and add products with no code, similar to signing up for Shopify. The difference shows up once you want something a standard theme cannot do: WooCommerce's checkout, templates and database are open PHP code that a developer can edit directly, while Shopify's customization happens through its own Liquid templating language and app store on Shopify's infrastructure. A store that only needs a normal catalog and checkout will not notice much difference day to day. One that wants a custom product configurator or a nonstandard checkout flow will need a developer on either platform, but only WooCommerce hands that developer the full underlying code to work with.

items.q: Does WooCommerce charge a transaction fee the way Shopify does?
items.a: No. WooCommerce's own pricing page states a 0% platform fee, and that applies no matter which payment gateway processes the sale. Shopify only avoids its own transaction fee when a store uses Shopify Payments, Shop Pay or PayPal Express Checkout; picking a different payment gateway on Shopify adds a charge of 2% on Basic, 1% on Grow or 0.6% on Advanced, on top of that gateway's own processing rate. WooCommerce's own payment processor, WooPayments, is not free of extra charges, though: it adds 1.5% for a card issued outside the US, another 1% when the customer pays in a different currency than your payout account, and a flat $15 for every disputed charge. The real difference is that Shopify can charge extra for choosing a different gateway, and WooCommerce cannot.

items.q: Is Shopify or WooCommerce better for a store that sells in person too?
items.a: Shopify, for most stores that split time between an online store and a physical counter. Shopify POS is built into every plan for casual in-person selling, and POS Pro adds advanced tools such as unlimited staff roles and in-store inventory for $89 per location a month. WooCommerce has no built-in point-of-sale system: selling in person means adding a separate POS extension and card reader on top of the core plugin and hosting, and WooCommerce's own pages do not publish a price for that setup. A retailer whose business is mostly walk-in, with an online store on the side, will generally find Shopify's bundled POS simpler to set up and support than assembling an equivalent on WooCommerce.

items.q: What happens if I stop paying for a WooCommerce extension?
items.a: The extension keeps working, but you stop getting updates and support. WooCommerce Marketplace extensions, such as WooCommerce Subscriptions at $279 a year or Bookings at $249 a year, are sold as yearly subscriptions that auto-renew by default and each cover one live site plus one staging site. If a renewal payment fails, WooCommerce retries it for about 26 days before the subscription actually expires, and even then the extension code stays installed and keeps working; only security updates and support stop. Every extension and theme on the Woo Marketplace also carries a 30-day money-back guarantee from the date of purchase, so a wrong pick can be refunded in full within that window. A renewal charges the full list price in force at that time, not whatever rate you first paid, and coupons do not apply to it. Shopify has no equivalent per-feature subscription to lapse, since its comparable costs sit inside the monthly plan price itself.
